newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Strike wreaks havoc with Colombian exports, food.
newsitem.headline: Strike wreaks havoc with Colombian exports, food.

text.p: Truck drivers on Wednesday entered the third day of a crippling nationwide stoppage that has clamped a virtual stranglehold on Colombia's economy.

Exporters say the strike has halted all shipments of coffee and other key commodities to Colombia's ports, and the only exports leaving the country since Monday are those traditionally sent by air freight, such as cut flowers.
Juan Carlos Aldana, head of Colombia's Port Authority, said imports had also been affected by the strike since truckers were refusing to move any merchandise inland from the country's ports.
In an interview with El Tiempo, Colombia's leading daily, Aldana added that there would be no refrigerator or storage space left in the country's ports if the strike continued into next week.

In addition to exporters and importers, the strike has put a squeeze on ordinary Colombians since prices for basic foodstuffs like potatoes, onions and yucca have skyrocketed on the back of dwindling supply.

Transportation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez has insisted that the strike posed no major threat to the economy, since government figures showed that only about 26,000 trucks had been pulled off the country's highways because of it.

But Olga Rosero Legarda, a leader of the Colombian Truck Drivers Association, insisted in a Reuter interview that the real number was closer to 100,000, or about 90 percent of Colombia's entire fleet of cargo vehicles.

The Drivers Association called the strike, which began at midnight on Sunday, to press for higher tariffs, lower taxes and tolls, and tighter security on highways. It is also insisting that the government lift a recent ban on cargo vehicles that are more than 16 years old.

Rosero said Lopez had called a meeting at the Transportation Ministry later on Wednesday afternoon to discuss a possible settlement of the strike. She added that union officials had no idea what sort of a deal Lopez would offer, however, and said the work stoppage would continue until a list of 19 demands had been satisfied one by one.
No violence has been reported in connection with the strike so far.
A train that carries coal from the El Cerrejon mine in northern Guajira province to Puerto Bolivar on the Caribbean coast was derailed by a bomb attack early on Wednesday.

No deaths or serious injuries were caused by the bomb, which caused two locomotives and 11 freight cars to jump the tracks. Police said they suspected it was the work of leftist guerrillas rather than strikers who have barricaded roads across the Guajira in a bid to block coal exports.
